# Pilot Capture Runbook

This follows the exact order the app gives you, because it is generated from the same ordering
code. Working down this page and working through the app's NEXT ACTION are the same sequence:
front-facing frames before the garment is turned over, everything that shares a camera height
and lens together, all the ruler macros in one run, and the required re-lays kept apart
because they are the measurement rather than an overhead.

Times are the specification's DECLARED planning figures. Nobody has yet timed this rig, and
the app replaces them with your own measured pace once it has three observations of a step
class. Treat the totals as an order of magnitude.

## What the whole pilot comes to

| state | frames | required | declared time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rig calibration | 28 | 27 | 1 h 32 min |
| Garment intake | 37 | 37 | 1 h 16 min |
| Before cut | 148 | 147 | 4 h 12 min |
| Marked for cutting | 10 | 10 | 15 min |
| Immediately after cutting | 30 | 30 | 42 min |
| Offcuts before wash | 30 | 30 | 32 min |
| After washing | 106 | 94 | 2 h 46 min |
| Offcuts after wash | 30 | 30 | 32 min |
| **total** | **419** | **405** | **11 h 57 min** |

That total is the most demanding garment the plan can describe: every optional feature present
and one instance of each. A plain pair with no paint, no repairs and no coin pocket is
materially shorter, and the app tells you your own number after intake.


### Rig calibration — either face, lay 1, handheld_free, main lens

- [ ] `RIG.BACKDROP.IDENTITY` (1/1, required)
      Handheld, close: the backdrop material with a hand-written card lying on it naming
      material, colour, supplier and date, plus a steel rule showing a 100 mm span across
      the weave. Card text and rule graduations must both be legible in this one frame.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §1's Background is an unfilled [FILL]. The written answer and the physical object are two different claims; protocol_audit only ever sees the text. This photograph is the only thing that binds the sentence in PROTOCOL.md to the surface actually under the garment, so a later session can prove it used the same backdrop rather than a similar one.
- [ ] `RIG.CAMERA.HEIGHT_RECORD` (1/2, required)
      A second camera or a mirror shot: tape measure standing on the backdrop surface with
      its zero touching the surface, running up to the mounted phone's rear lens. One
      frame must show the tape reading at the lens plane AND enough of the phone body to
      prove it is the mounted phone. Reading legible to 5 mm.
      *why:* Mount height is the one rig parameter that is unrecoverable from the photographs afterwards and the one that converts fabric thickness into a scale error (2t/H, see RIG.PLANE.COPLANAR_GRAZING). It also sets the field of view, and therefore whether the garment and the board both fit while still resolving 800 px of waistband. It is an unfilled [FILL] that the existing audit silently cannot see.
- [ ] `RIG.CAMERA.HEIGHT_RECORD` (2/2, required)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**
      A second camera or a mirror shot: tape measure standing on the backdrop surface with
      its zero touching the surface, running up to the mounted phone's rear lens. One
      frame must show the tape reading at the lens plane AND enough of the phone body to
      prove it is the mounted phone. Reading legible to 5 mm.
      *why:* Mount height is the one rig parameter that is unrecoverable from the photographs afterwards and the one that converts fabric thickness into a scale error (2t/H, see RIG.PLANE.COPLANAR_GRAZING). It also sets the field of view, and therefore whether the garment and the board both fit while still resolving 800 px of waistband. It is an unfilled [FILL] that the existing audit silently cannot see.
- [ ] `RIG.CAMERA.LEVEL_INDICATOR` (1/1, optional)
      Photograph of the mounted phone's own level / horizon overlay on screen, with the
      two crosshairs coincident, taken without touching the mount.
      *why:* Cheap corroboration for the single most consequential and least observable rig parameter. EXP_0021 measured that 6 of 16 real subjects lose more than 5% of a shape ratio below 5 degrees of tilt, one at 1 degree, and that tilt is invisible in the photograph. Having two instruments disagree is worth more than having one instrument that cannot be checked.
- [ ] `RIG.CAMERA.SETTINGS_SCREEN` (1/1, required)
      Photograph of the phone's camera screen, mounted and aimed at the rig, showing
      simultaneously: the selected lens multiplier (0.5x / 1x / 2x), the AE lock and AWB
      lock indicators engaged, the capture format setting, and the capture resolution. All
      four legible in one frame.
      *why:* Two settings can invalidate an entire session and both are invisible in the resulting files until it is too late to reshoot: a HEIC container that this toolchain cannot open, and an unlocked auto-exposure that makes the before and after frames incomparable. PROTOCOL §1 names the phone model as an unfilled [FILL] and says 'locked exposure/WB' with no evidence requirement. This is that evidence, taken before the first garment frame rather than discovered after the cut.
- [ ] `RIG.OBLIQUE.STATION_MARKS` (1/1, required)
      Handheld from above and behind the rig showing all four taped oblique stations
      (front-left, front-right, back-left, back-right) on the floor or table edge, with a
      tape measure laid from the backdrop centreline to each mark so the offsets are
      readable. All four marks and at least two readings in one frame; take a second frame
      if four readings will not fit.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §2 specifies obliques 'at ~30 degrees' and gives no way to stand in the same place twice. The obliques' entire value is cross-state comparison, so an unreproducible station makes 16 shots per state into 16 shots that cannot be compared with anything. Marking the stations costs four minutes once and is the only thing that makes matched_shot_ids meaningful for the oblique series.

### Rig calibration — either face, lay 1, handheld_grazing_surface, main lens

- [ ] `RIG.PLANE.COPLANAR_GRAZING` (1/1, required)
      Lens axis within about 10 mm of the backdrop surface, sighting ALONG the surface so
      the surface reads as a single line across the frame. A rigid straightedge at least
      as long as the board's 295 mm axis lies across the board and continues onto the bare
      backdrop where the garment's waistband will lie. The straightedge's full span and
      both ends must be in frame, with the surface line visible underneath along the whole
      length.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §1 requires the board on the same surface plane as the garment, and nothing overhead can check it: a top-down frame cannot show a height difference, which is the same blindness EXP_0021 documented for camera tilt. A board 5 mm proud of the backdrop on a 1 m mount is a 0.5% scale error applied to every measurement — larger than the print tolerance and completely invisible in F00. A grazing view is the only cheap instrument that turns an out-of-plane offset into something a person can see.

### Rig calibration — either face, lay 1, handheld_macro_close, macro lens

- [ ] `RIG.BOARD.PRINT_SCALE_LONG` (1/2, required)
      Camera perpendicular to the board. A steel rule with 1 mm graduations lies ON the
      printed board with its measuring edge passing through the two extreme interior
      chessboard corners of the long (11-square) axis. Both extreme corners and the rule
      graduations at both ends must be legible in this single frame; do not stitch two
      frames.
      *why:* Every millimetre this project reports comes from square_mm = 25.0 in protocol/charuco_board.json, which is a statement about a PDF, not about the sheet of paper on the table. Consumer printers scale by fractions of a percent and 'fit to page' silently rescales. If the print is 1% small, every mm_per_px, every measurement and the cut position itself are 1% wrong, consistently, and nothing downstream can detect it because the error is common to all frames. Two independent readings follow PROTOCOL §0.4's own 'two readings each' convention.
- [ ] `RIG.BOARD.PRINT_SCALE_LONG` (2/2, required)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**
      Camera perpendicular to the board. A steel rule with 1 mm graduations lies ON the
      printed board with its measuring edge passing through the two extreme interior
      chessboard corners of the long (11-square) axis. Both extreme corners and the rule
      graduations at both ends must be legible in this single frame; do not stitch two
      frames.
      *why:* Every millimetre this project reports comes from square_mm = 25.0 in protocol/charuco_board.json, which is a statement about a PDF, not about the sheet of paper on the table. Consumer printers scale by fractions of a percent and 'fit to page' silently rescales. If the print is 1% small, every mm_per_px, every measurement and the cut position itself are 1% wrong, consistently, and nothing downstream can detect it because the error is common to all frames. Two independent readings follow PROTOCOL §0.4's own 'two readings each' convention.
- [ ] `RIG.BOARD.PRINT_SCALE_SHORT` (1/2, required)
      As RIG.BOARD.PRINT_SCALE_LONG but across the short (8-square) axis: rule edge
      through the two extreme interior corners of that axis, both corners and both end
      graduations legible in one frame.
      *why:* Printers scale differently along and across the paper feed direction. A single-axis check cannot see anisotropic print scaling, and anisotropic scale is worse than isotropic: mm_per_pixel() takes a MEDIAN over adjacent-corner spacings in both directions, so an anisotropic print returns a plausible single number that is wrong in both axes and right in neither. This is the only frame that can falsify that.
- [ ] `RIG.BOARD.PRINT_SCALE_SHORT` (2/2, required)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**
      As RIG.BOARD.PRINT_SCALE_LONG but across the short (8-square) axis: rule edge
      through the two extreme interior corners of that axis, both corners and both end
      graduations legible in one frame.
      *why:* Printers scale differently along and across the paper feed direction. A single-axis check cannot see anisotropic print scaling, and anisotropic scale is worse than isotropic: mm_per_pixel() takes a MEDIAN over adjacent-corner spacings in both directions, so an anisotropic print returns a plausible single number that is wrong in both axes and right in neither. This is the only frame that can falsify that.

### Rig calibration — either face, lay 1, mount_grazing_table, tele lens

- [ ] `RIG.STATION.GRAZING_CERTIFY.SIDE` (1/2, required)
      At the grazing station, a small vertical steel rule stood on the capture surface at
      the frame centre, its 0 mm mark touching the surface, and a straight dark card laid
      flat running left-right through the frame to make the surface line visible. Camera
      optical axis in the surface plane (lens centre 20-40 mm above the surface), pointing
      horizontally, perpendicular to the card's long edge. The rule's 0-50 mm span and the
      surface line must both be sharp and both must cross the frame centre.
      *why:* Edge curl is a displacement normal to the capture surface and has no metric anchor at all unless the grazing station's vertical scale and axis horizontality are certified separately. The overhead board's mm_per_px is the wrong scale for anything lifted out of the surface plane, so curl cannot borrow it.
- [ ] `RIG.STATION.GRAZING_CERTIFY.SIDE` (2/2, required)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**

      optical axis in the surface plane (lens centre 20-40 mm above the surface), pointing
      horizontally, perpendicular to the card's long edge. The rule's 0-50 mm span and the
      surface line must both be sharp and both must cross the frame centre.
      *why:* Edge curl is a displacement normal to the capture surface and has no metric anchor at all unless the grazing station's vertical scale and axis horizontality are certified separately. The overhead board's mm_per_px is the wrong scale for anything lifted out of the surface plane, so curl cannot borrow it.

### Rig calibration — either face, lay 1, mount_low_macro, tele lens

- [ ] `RIG.STATION.MACRO_RESOLUTION.TARGET` (1/2, required)
      At the macro station, with the mount, lens and working distance exactly as they will
      be for the hem macros, place the certified loop tape flat where the cut edge will
      lie and shoot it filling the frame: about 100 mm of graduated tape across the
      frame's long dimension, tape plane perpendicular to the optical axis. Nothing else
      in frame. Repeat if the working distance, lens or crop mode changes.
      *why:* Machine-checkable proof that the macro station resolves 0.5 mm fray depth. Post-wash macros cannot be retaken after the garment is re-handled without disturbing the fringe, so the resolution ceiling has to be demonstrated on a target first. Without it, an under-resolved loop map looks protocol-compliant and answers nothing - the exact failure EXP_0016 records for the found pairs at 241-389 px of waistband.
- [ ] `RIG.STATION.MACRO_RESOLUTION.TARGET` (2/2, required)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**
      At the macro station, with the mount, lens and working distance exactly as they will
      be for the hem macros, place the certified loop tape flat where the cut edge will
      lie and shoot it filling the frame: about 100 mm of graduated tape across the
      frame's long dimension, tape plane perpendicular to the optical axis. Nothing else
      in frame. Repeat if the working distance, lens or crop mode changes.
      *why:* Machine-checkable proof that the macro station resolves 0.5 mm fray depth. Post-wash macros cannot be retaken after the garment is re-handled without disturbing the fringe, so the resolution ceiling has to be demonstrated on a target first. Without it, an under-resolved loop map looks protocol-compliant and answers nothing - the exact failure EXP_0016 records for the found pairs at 241-389 px of waistband.

### Rig calibration — either face, lay 1, mount_mid_overhead_hem, main lens

- [ ] `RIG.SCALE.TAPE_CERTIFY.OVERHEAD` (1/2, required)
      The flexible loop-coordinate tape (a printed or steel mm tape, the one that will lie
      beside the cut edge for every MACRO) laid dead flat on the capture surface
      immediately beside the printed ChArUco board, both fully inside the frame, tape
      graduations facing the camera, at least 200 mm of tape visible. Frame the board+tape
      pair so at least 12 interior board corners are resolved. Shoot once per capture
      session and once again if the tape is bent, replaced or reprinted.
      *why:* Establishes the scale chain the entire hem programme rests on. The fray-depth, thread-count and edge-curl measurands all need mm/px inside a 100 mm frame, and the ChArUco board physically cannot fit there, so scale must be transferred by a physical object that appears in both a board-bearing frame and every macro. Without this frame every macro's mm_per_px is an unverified human assertion and the whole loop map degrades to HUMAN_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED.
- [ ] `RIG.SCALE.TAPE_CERTIFY.OVERHEAD` (2/2, required)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**
      The flexible loop-coordinate tape (a printed or steel mm tape, the one that will lie
      beside the cut edge for every MACRO) laid dead flat on the capture surface

      graduations facing the camera, at least 200 mm of tape visible. Frame the board+tape
      pair so at least 12 interior board corners are resolved. Shoot once per capture

### Rig calibration — either face, lay 1, mount_overhead_locked, main lens

- [ ] `RIG.BACKDROP.EMPTY` (1/1, required)
      From the locked overhead mount, the bare backdrop only: no board, no garment, no
      ruler, no hand. The backdrop must reach every frame edge — no wall, table edge,
      floor seam, cable or operator shadow anywhere in frame.
      *why:* quality.py estimates background colour from an 8 px frame-border ring and splits foreground by Lab distance to that median. Every garment verdict in the whole pilot rests on that assumption. This frame is the only evidence that the assumption holds — that the backdrop is one colour, unclipped and free of a gradient the border ring cannot see. Without it a lighting hotspot or a visible table edge silently biases foreground_fraction, mean_intensity and border_fraction on all 4 states.
- [ ] `RIG.BOARD.FLAT_OVERHEAD` (1/1, required)
      From the locked overhead mount, bare backdrop with the printed ChArUco board lying
      flat in the frame corner it will occupy for the rest of the project (PROTOCOL §1:
      'same corner of the frame every time'). Whole board inside the frame with at least
      50 mm of backdrop beyond every board edge; no garment, no hand, no ruler.
      *why:* Three things at once, none of which any later frame can establish. It is the only frame where enough of the board is resolved to fit a pose, so it is the only measurement of whether the mount is actually square to the surface — the error EXP_0021 showed is invisible in the photograph and costs >5% of every shape ratio. It fixes the frozen board position PROTOCOL §1 demands. And its mm_per_px is the rig's nominal scale, against which a garment frame's scale can be sanity-checked instead of being trusted blind.
- [ ] `RIG.DAYLIGHT.CONTROLLED` (1/2, required)
      From the locked mount with BOTH rig lights switched off and the exposure and white
      balance still at the locked session values. Bare backdrop with the board in its
      frozen corner, room exactly as it will be during capture — blinds, doors and screens
      in their working positions. Rep 1 immediately before the session's first garment
      frame, rep 2 immediately after its last.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §1 freezes the lamps and is silent about the sun. A full state takes hours, daylight moves through them, and its contribution is invisible in any single frame because the lamps swamp it. Two ambient-only frames bracketing the session are the only measurement of how much of the light was uncontrolled and whether it changed — which is precisely the confound that would make a post-wash colour or shading difference look like an effect of the wash.
- [ ] `RIG.DAYLIGHT.CONTROLLED` (2/2, required)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**
      From the locked mount with BOTH rig lights switched off and the exposure and white
      balance still at the locked session values. Bare backdrop with the board in its
      frozen corner, room exactly as it will be during capture — blinds, doors and screens
      in their working positions. Rep 1 immediately before the session's first garment
      frame, rep 2 immediately after its last.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §1 freezes the lamps and is silent about the sun. A full state takes hours, daylight moves through them, and its contribution is invisible in any single frame because the lamps swamp it. Two ambient-only frames bracketing the session are the only measurement of how much of the light was uncontrolled and whether it changed — which is precisely the confound that would make a post-wash colour or shading difference look like an effect of the wash.
- [ ] `RIG.EXPOSURE.GREY_CARD` (1/1, required)
      From the locked mount with exposure and white balance LOCKED at the values that will
      be used for the whole session. Neutral grey card flat at the centre of the garment
      footprint, filling at least a quarter of the frame's short dimension. The ChArUco
      board must be in its frozen corner in the same frame.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §1 says 'locked exposure/WB' and provides no way to check the lock held. The grey card is the only object in the rig whose correct rendering is known in advance, so it is the only reference against which a later session's exposure and colour can be compared at all. Without it, a drifted white balance between the before and the post-wash state reads as a change in the garment — exactly the false positive the whole before/after design is meant to exclude.
- [ ] `RIG.LIGHTING.CARD_SWEEP` (1/5, required)
      Five frames from the locked mount with the camera, exposure and white balance
      untouched throughout. One frame per neutral-card position: (1) centre of the garment
      footprint, then (2)-(5) each of the four corners of that footprint. The card lies
      flat and must fill at least a quarter of the frame's short dimension in every
      position.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §1 freezes 'two diffuse sources at ~45 degrees', which constrains direction and says nothing about uniformity over a 1.1 m footprint. A single empty-backdrop frame cannot separate an illumination gradient from the backdrop's own reflectance variation and from lens vignetting — they are confounded. Moving one card of fixed reflectance through five positions is the only way to isolate the light. It matters because check_image judges garment exposure by a single mean over the whole foreground, so a thigh lit 30% brighter than a hem passes as correctly exposed while the hem — the thing this project exists to measure — is underexposed.
- [ ] `RIG.LIGHTING.CARD_SWEEP` (2/5, required)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**

      untouched throughout. One frame per neutral-card position: (1) centre of the garment
      footprint, then (2)-(5) each of the four corners of that footprint. The card lies
      flat and must fill at least a quarter of the frame's short dimension in every

- [ ] `RIG.LAY.GAP_TEMPLATE` (1/1, required)
      From the locked mount, bare backdrop with the frozen leg-centreline marks in place
      and a rule laid across the gap between them showing the gap in cm. Board in its
      frozen corner. Marks must lie inside the frame but OUTSIDE both the 8 px frame-
      border ring and the rectangle the garment will occupy.
      *why:* The five F00 repetitions measure re-lay variance, and that number is only interpretable if each re-lay was aiming at the same target. A remembered gap is not a target. Marking the frozen leg centrelines physically converts 'legs spread by the frozen gap' from an instruction into something reproducible, and it is what makes the legs-never-touching requirement checkable by eye at capture time instead of by segmentation afterwards — segmentation being UNAVAILABLE without torch, segment_anything and the 375 MB SAM checkpoint.

### Garment intake — FRONT up, lay 1, handheld_macro_close, macro lens

- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.BELT_LOOPS.WAISTBAND_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_belt_loops)
      Front waistband spanning from the fly to the garment-left side seam, showing every
      belt loop on that span with its top and bottom bartacks, camera perpendicular, rule
      laid along the waistband in the fabric plane. Repeat as a second frame for the fly-
      to-right-side-seam span if the loops will not fit in one.
      *why:* Belt loops are the only structures rigidly attached across the waistband's top edge, which is the structure the 800 px resolution floor is defined on. Their spacing is a directly measurable, wash-sensitive length along the waistband, and unlike the waistband edge itself it does not depend on how hard the garment was smoothed.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.FLY.FLY_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_button_fly or has_zip_fly)
      Whole fly from the waistband button down to the bottom of the fly stitch, closed,
      camera perpendicular, rule alongside in the fabric plane. Button or every fly
      button, the fly topstitch curve, and the bar tack at the bottom must all be in
      frame.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §0.4 defines front rise as 'crotch seam to top of waistband along the fly', so the fly is literally the measurement path for one of the seven registered dimensions. A frame that resolves the fly's ends in millimetres is the only evidence that the tape followed the path the measurement_convention const describes, rather than a straight line across the fabric.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.RIVETS.POCKET_FRONT_RIGHT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_rivets)
      One rivet per frame, rivet centred and filling at least a fifth of the frame short
      dimension, camera perpendicular to the denim around it, rule in the fabric plane
      alongside. Include enough surrounding denim to identify which seam or pocket corner
      the rivet sits on.
      *why:* Rivets are the only rigid, dimensionally stable objects sewn into the garment, so the pixel distance between two rivets is a length that fabric shrinkage cannot change. That makes rivet-to-rivet spacing an internal scale check on any frame containing two of them — independent of the board, and therefore able to catch the case where the board has moved out of the garment's plane. They also matter for a completely different reason: scale_from_coin.py refuses an unmasked frame precisely because rivets read as coins under Hough.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.COIN_POCKET.POCKET_COIN_RIGHT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_coin_pocket or has_watch_pocket_rivets)
      Coin/watch pocket filling at least half the frame short dimension, camera
      perpendicular to the fabric, rule in the fabric's plane alongside. The pocket's full
      opening, both bartacks or rivets, and at least 20 mm of surrounding denim on every
      side must be in frame.
      *why:* The coin pocket and its rivets are the densest cluster of hard points on the front panel and they sit high on the thigh, above any plausible jorts cut line. They therefore survive the cut unchanged and act as a fixed reference against which the post-wash front panel can be checked for shrinkage and displacement — a control region whose appearance the wash should not change.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.ASYMMETRY.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_asymmetry)
      Both hems brought together side by side, edges aligned against a straightedge,
      camera perpendicular, rule laid across both in the fabric plane, so any difference
      in leg length or leg opening between the two legs is directly visible and measurable
      in one frame.
      *why:* Comparing the two legs within a single frame removes the photography from the comparison entirely — the same lens, the same light, the same instant. Comparing them across two frames does not, and at the millimetre scale that matters here the difference between the two methods is the whole measurement. Since the legs are cut separately, an unrecorded asymmetry becomes an asymmetry in the jorts that will be indistinguishable from cutting error.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.DECORATIVE_HARDWARE.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_decorative_hardware)
      One hardware item per frame (buckle, chain, D-ring, decorative button, zip pull),
      item centred with at least 20 mm of surrounding fabric, camera perpendicular to the
      fabric plane, rule alongside in that plane.
      *why:* Hardware is the class of feature most likely to be damaged by the wash and most likely to damage the garment during it, and it changes the load's mechanical behaviour. It is also the feature most likely to break a segmentation: a bright metal item on dark denim is a large Lab distance from the backdrop and can dominate an Otsu split. Recording each item is what allows a later mask failure to be attributed rather than guessed at.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.DISTRESSING.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_distressing > 0)
      One distressed area per frame — abrasion, whiskering, honeycomb, a worn-through
      patch — filling at least half the frame with at least 30 mm of intact denim visible
      on every side so the boundary between distressed and intact fabric is in frame.
      Camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane.
      *why:* Distressed areas are thin, so they shrink and abrade differently from the surrounding fabric and are where wash-induced change is largest. They are also the project's known segmentation hazard: EXP_0016's addendum found that both of its two false 'frayed' readings on finished hems were SAM dropping blobs of strongly bleached or patterned denim, not hems at all. Recording where the thin fabric is, at intake, is what makes a later mask failure diagnosable rather than mysterious.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.EMBROIDERY.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_embroidery > 0)
      One embroidered element per frame, close enough that individual stitches are
      resolved, with the surrounding denim visible on at least three sides. Camera
      perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane.
      *why:* Embroidery is a dense, stiff thread mass on a fabric that shrinks around it, so it puckers after the first wash and produces a localised out-of-plane deformation on an otherwise flat garment. On a flat-lay that pucker lifts the fabric off the backdrop, which changes the local scale and can lift the surrounding denim out of the board's plane — the one assumption RIG.PLANE.COPLANAR_GRAZING exists to protect.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.LOGOS.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_logos > 0)
      One logo per frame — printed, woven, heat-transferred or applied — filling at least
      half the frame short dimension, with surrounding denim on at least three sides.
      Camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane.
      *why:* Applied logos are heat-transfer or plastisol films that crack, lift or lose gloss in the first wash independently of anything happening to the denim. Recorded at intake, each one is an appearance change with a known before state; unrecorded, they are differences between the before and post-wash frames with no explanation, in a project whose whole claim is about explaining such differences.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.PAINT.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_paint > 0)
      One painted area per frame, showing an edge of the paint and the bare denim beside
      it in the same frame, plus any existing cracking or flaking of the paint film.
      Camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane, at least 30 mm of bare denim
      visible.
      *why:* A paint film is the feature most likely to be changed by the wash and the feature whose change is most likely to be mistaken for something else — cracking, flaking and edge lift all alter the garment's appearance without any fabric having moved. It is also a wash-branch determinant under PROTOCOL §7 rather than merely an appearance record, so it must be captured before the wash is planned, not alongside it.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.PATCHES.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_patches > 0)
      One patch per frame, showing the whole patch, its full attachment perimeter
      (stitched, glued or fused), and the denim it sits on. Camera perpendicular, rule in
      the fabric plane, at least 20 mm margin.
      *why:* A patch is an added layer with its own shrinkage and its own attachment that may not survive the wash. If it detaches, the garment's outline changes, and every shape ratio computed from the post-wash silhouette changes with it — a large effect with a mundane cause that must be attributable to the patch rather than absorbed into the model's error.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.PREVIOUS_ALTERATION.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_previous_alteration)
      One alteration per frame (taken-in seam, shortened leg, replaced waistband, re-
      stitched hem), showing the altered structure and enough of the original construction
      either side of it that the join is visible. Camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric
      plane, at least 30 mm margin.
      *why:* A previously shortened or taken-in garment is not the garment its size chart or its style number describes, and the alteration's thread, stitch density and seam allowance differ from the factory's — so it shrinks and frays differently from the fabric around it. On a secondhand pilot garment this is the most likely silent violation of the assumption that the before state is an unmodified baseline.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.PRINTED_FADE.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_printed_fade > 0)
      One printed or laser-etched fade region per frame, framed so both the lightest and
      the darkest part of the pattern and a margin of un-patterned denim are all inside
      the frame. Camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane.
      *why:* A printed fade mimics genuine wear and is exactly the appearance this project is trying to predict, so it must not be mistaken for it. It is also a direct threat to the measurement layer: EXP_0016's two false 'frayed' readings on finished hems were both strongly patterned denim where SAM dropped large blobs of the leg. Recording where the pattern is at intake is what allows a later mask failure over it to be attributed rather than argued about.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.REPAIRS.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_repairs > 0)
      One repair per frame (darn, patch-behind, sashiko, machine bartack), showing the
      repair, its stitch density, and the intact fabric it joins on at least three sides.
      Camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane.
      *why:* A repair is a stiff, densely stitched region with different shrinkage from the fabric around it, so it puckers or pulls after the first wash and produces a local shape change that has nothing to do with cutting. Without a recorded before state, that pucker is an unexplained difference between the before and post-wash frames.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.STAINS.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_stains > 0)
      One stain per frame, with unstained denim of the same panel visible in the same
      frame for comparison. Camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane, at least 30 mm
      of clean denim on at least two sides.
      *why:* Stains are the one existing feature expected to CHANGE in the wash, and a stain that lifts is a large, obvious appearance difference between the before and post-wash frames that has nothing to do with cutting. Measured against adjacent clean denim inside the same frame, its before state is recorded in a way that does not depend on the two sessions having matched exposure.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.TEARS.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_tears > 0)
      One tear or hole per frame, with a contrasting card slipped behind it so the
      opening's true outline is visible rather than reading as the fabric behind. Camera
      perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane, at least 30 mm of intact denim on every
      side.
      *why:* An existing tear is a raw edge that has already been washed, so it is the one place on the garment that shows how THIS fabric frays — the closest thing available to a prediction of what the cut edge will do, recorded before the cut is made. Its loose threads also grow in the wash, which makes it an internal positive control for the fray measurement alongside the factory hem's negative control.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.UNUSUAL_SEAMS.WHOLE_GARMENT_FRONT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_unusual_seams)
      One unusual seam per frame (twisted, offset, non-standard felled, contrast-stitched,
      panelled), showing at least 100 mm of its run and its relationship to the nearest
      standard seam. Camera perpendicular, rule along the seam in the fabric plane.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §3.1 freezes the cut as perpendicular to the leg's centre line, the midline between inseam and outseam. A twisted or offset seam moves that midline away from where a symmetric model puts it, so the frozen cut definition lands somewhere other than intended. This frame is the evidence that the centre line used for the cut was the garment's actual one.

### Garment intake — FRONT up, lay 1, mount_overhead_locked, main lens

- [ ] `INTAKE.WHOLE.FRONT_OVERHEAD_ASIS` (1/1, required)
      From the locked mount, garment AS RECEIVED, front up, waistband at the top of frame
      — laid out but deliberately NOT smoothed, NOT pressed and NOT arranged to the frozen
      gap. Whole garment inside the frame with visible backdrop on all four sides; board
      in its frozen corner.
      *why:* Two jobs. It is the permanent record of the garment's condition on arrival — creases, storage folds, prior pressing — which no later frame can recover because the lay protocol destroys it. And it is the ENUMERATION REFERENCE for every front-panel feature instance: instance ordinals are assigned by centroid position in this exact frame, so the numbering is deterministic and permanent rather than depending on the order the operator happened to notice things.

### Garment intake — either face, lay 1, handheld_grazing_surface, main lens

- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.HEM_CURL.HEM_LEFT_FRONT.I01` (1/2, conditional, has_hem_curl_visible)
      Lens axis within about 10 mm of the backdrop surface, sighting ALONG the surface at
      the hem edge so the surface reads as a line. Garment laid front-up and flat, hem
      edge toward the camera. Rule standing vertically on the surface immediately behind
      the hem, graduations facing the camera, so any lift of the edge off the surface is
      read directly against it.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §5 defines edge curl as 'max vertical lift of the hem edge from the surface', a purely out-of-plane quantity that an overhead frame cannot see at all. This is its pre-cut, pre-wash baseline: without it, any curl measured after the wash is an absolute number with nothing to be a change from, and a garment that arrived with a curled hem would be scored as having curled in the wash.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.HEM_CURL.HEM_LEFT_FRONT.I01` (2/2, conditional, has_hem_curl_visible)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**
      Lens axis within about 10 mm of the backdrop surface, sighting ALONG the surface at
      the hem edge so the surface reads as a line. Garment laid front-up and flat, hem
      edge toward the camera. Rule standing vertically on the surface immediately behind
      the hem, graduations facing the camera, so any lift of the edge off the surface is
      read directly against it.
      *why:* PROTOCOL §5 defines edge curl as 'max vertical lift of the hem edge from the surface', a purely out-of-plane quantity that an overhead frame cannot see at all. This is its pre-cut, pre-wash baseline: without it, any curl measured after the wash is an absolute number with nothing to be a change from, and a garment that arrived with a curled hem would be scored as having curled in the wash.

### Garment intake — either face, lay 1, handheld_macro_close, macro lens

- [ ] `INTAKE.LABEL.CARE_BACK` (1/1, conditional, has_care_label)
      Lift the care label and support it flat with its reverse face up, camera
      perpendicular, rule alongside in the same plane. If the reverse is genuinely blank,
      photograph it blank — do not skip the shot.
      *why:* Care labels routinely carry the fibre composition on one face and the wash symbols on the other, and a photograph of one face read as the whole label produces a confident, wrong composition. Photographing the reverse unconditionally — including when it is blank — is what makes the absence of further text a recorded observation instead of an assumption.
- [ ] `INTAKE.LABEL.CARE_FRONT` (1/1, conditional, has_care_label)
      Care label held flat (clip it or weight its corners; do not stretch it), camera
      perpendicular to the label face, label filling most of the frame with a steel rule
      alongside in the same plane showing at least 30 mm of graduations. Every printed
      line of the label must be legible at 100% zoom.
      *why:* This single photograph decides two things nothing else can. It supplies fiber_composition and elastane_percentage, two of the schema's seven required fields. And it decides is_machine_washable, which selects the entire §4 wash branch and, through PROTOCOL §7, which offcut carries the standard-protocol data point — the branch DENIM_0001 has already taken. It must therefore precede every wash decision, and it is irreversible in the sense that a label lost in the wash cannot be re-photographed.
- [ ] `INTAKE.LABEL.CARE_STACK_SPREAD` (1/1, conditional, has_second_care_label)
      Fan the whole stack of sewn-in labels apart so every individual label in the stack
      is separately visible and countable in one frame, rule alongside in the same plane.
      *why:* Where labels are stacked, the composition is often on the third one down and the top one is a brand tag. A frame that proves how many labels exist is what turns 'the composition is X' into a claim that can be re-checked, and it is the only defence against transcribing the wrong tag.
- [ ] `INTAKE.LABEL.INTERIOR_STAMP` (1/1, conditional, has_interior_stamp)
      Interior stamp, ink mark, or printed pocket bag turned out and held flat, camera
      perpendicular, rule alongside in the same plane, all characters legible at 100%
      zoom.
      *why:* Interior stamps carry lot, factory and date codes that outlive a removed care label and are frequently the only remaining route to a garment's identity. On a used pilot garment bought secondhand, this is often the difference between a documented provenance and 'acquisition_source: thrift'.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.SELVEDGE.SEAM_OUTSEAM_LEFT.I01` (1/2, conditional, has_selvedge)
      Turn the garment-left leg's outseam open at the hem so the selvedge line and its
      coloured warp are visible, hold it flat, camera perpendicular, rule laid along the
      seam in the fabric plane. At least 100 mm of seam and the selvedge's woven edge must
      be in frame.
      *why:* A selvedge outseam is a woven edge that cannot fray in the way a cut edge does, so it is a within-garment negative control for the fray measurement: the same fabric, the same wash, an edge that must not read as frayed. Every fray control this project has used so far has been a different garment (EXP_0016's nine finished-hem flat-lays), which confounds edge finish with fabric, lighting and photographer. This is the only control that does not.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.SELVEDGE.SEAM_OUTSEAM_LEFT.I01` (2/2, conditional, has_selvedge)  **TAKE THE PHONE OFF THE MOUNT AND REMOUNT IT**
      Turn the garment-left leg's outseam open at the hem so the selvedge line and its
      coloured warp are visible, hold it flat, camera perpendicular, rule laid along the
      seam in the fabric plane. At least 100 mm of seam and the selvedge's woven edge must
      be in frame.
      *why:* A selvedge outseam is a woven edge that cannot fray in the way a cut edge does, so it is a within-garment negative control for the fray measurement: the same fabric, the same wash, an edge that must not read as frayed. Every fray control this project has used so far has been a different garment (EXP_0016's nine finished-hem flat-lays), which confounds edge finish with fabric, lighting and photographer. This is the only control that does not.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.CUFFS.HEM_LEFT_FRONT.I01` (1/2, conditional, has_cuffs)
      Two frames per leg: the cuff as received (rolled), then the SAME hem fully unrolled
      and flattened. Camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane, at least 100 mm of
      hem edge in frame in both.
      *why:* A cuff hides the true hem and shortens every length measured to it. Because the cut position is computed from the inseam and the cut is irreversible, a cuff mistaken for the hem is one of the few errors in this whole protocol that cannot be corrected after the fact. Photographing both states makes the correction auditable instead of remembered.

      Two frames per leg: the cuff as received (rolled), then the SAME hem fully unrolled

Because the cut position is computed from the inseam and the cut is irreversible, a cuff mistaken for the hem is one of the few errors in this whole protocol that cannot be corrected after the fact. Photographing both states makes the correction auditable instead of remembered.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.FACTORY_HEM.HEM_LEFT_FRONT.I01` (1/2, conditional, has_factory_hem)
      About 100 mm of the original factory hem filling the frame width, camera
      perpendicular to the fabric and parallel to the surface (not angled down at the
      hem), rule laid in the fabric plane immediately alongside the hem edge. The turned-
      and-topstitched edge, its stitch line, and at least 30 mm of denim above it must be
      in frame.
      *why:* This is the single most valuable control frame in Part A. A factory hem is a finished edge that physically cannot fray, on this garment, in this fabric, under this light, at this scale — the exact within-subject control every fray result in this project currently lacks. EXP_0016's zero-false-positive claim rests on nine finished hems from nine other garments, and EXP_0021 showed two of those nine flip to 'frayed' under a mere JPEG re-encode. Framed identically to the post-wash raw-edge close-up, this frame is what makes 'the cut edge frayed' a comparison rather than an assertion.

EXP_0016's zero-false-positive claim rests on nine finished hems from nine other garments, and EXP_0021 showed two of those nine flip to 'frayed' under a mere JPEG re-encode. Framed identically to the post-wash raw-edge close-up, this frame is what makes 'the cut edge frayed' a comparison rather than an assertion.
- [ ] `INTAKE.LABEL.SIZE_TAG` (1/1, conditional, has_size_tag)
      Size tag held flat, camera perpendicular, tag filling most of the frame with a rule
      alongside in the same plane. Any style or SKU number on the tag must be legible at
      100% zoom.
      *why:* The tag is the only route to a style or SKU, which is what makes a manufacturer size chart usable as a cross-check on the measured dimensions. It must stay strictly a cross-check: DENIM_0002's record shows what happens when a chart is trusted as a measurement — its thigh_cm 36.2 was converted from 14.25 in without the doubling its own measurement_convention const requires, while leg_opening_cm was doubled correctly, and the two errors sit in one committed file.

### Garment intake — BACK up, lay 1, handheld_macro_close, macro lens

- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.BELT_LOOPS.WAISTBAND_BACK.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_back_belt_loops)
      Back waistband centre span showing the centre belt loop and the loops either side of
      it, with the centre back seam visible, camera perpendicular, rule along the
      waistband in the fabric plane.
      *why:* The centre back loop marks the garment's own centreline, which is the reference the back-panel lay is squared to. Recording its position relative to the centre back seam gives an independent check that the back-up lay is not rotated relative to the front-up lay — a rotation that would otherwise be indistinguishable from camera tilt, the error EXP_0021 shows is invisible in the photograph.
- [ ] `INTAKE.LABEL.BRAND_PATCH` (1/1, conditional, has_brand_patch)
      Back waistband brand patch, camera perpendicular to the patch, patch filling at
      least half the frame short dimension, rule alongside in the fabric's plane. Include
      the two waistband seams above and below the patch so its position on the waistband
      is recoverable.
      *why:* A leather or jacron patch is the highest-contrast, most rigid object on the garment and it sits on the waistband — the exact structure whose 800 px span every resolution requirement is written against. It is therefore both a brand record and a fixed, non-deforming landmark that appears identically in the before and post-wash frames, which makes it useful for checking that the two frames really are the same garment laid the same way.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.YOKE.YOKE_BACK.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_yoke)
      Back yoke seam across its full width from outseam to outseam, camera perpendicular,
      rule laid along the seam in the fabric plane. Both ends of the yoke seam and the
      centre back seam junction must be in frame; take two overlapping frames if the full
      width will not resolve in one.
      *why:* The yoke is a horizontal double-thickness band running the full width of the back panel, so it is where differential shrinkage between one and two fabric layers is most visible after the first wash, and it is the structure that sets the back panel's curvature when the garment is laid flat. Its seam is also the most reliable horizontal reference on the back panel for checking that the back-up lay is square.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.BACK_POCKET.POCKET_BACK_LEFT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_back_pockets and has_left_back_pocket)
      Garment-LEFT back pocket (image LEFT in the back-up lay), whole pocket plus at least
      30 mm of surrounding denim, camera perpendicular, rule in the fabric plane. Both top
      corners, the full stitch pattern and any rivets must be in frame.
      *why:* Back pockets are the largest multi-layer stack on the garment (pocket + denim + often a hidden rivet), so they shrink differently from single-layer denim and pucker after the first wash. They are also seg/validate's classic false positive — EXP_0018 records SAM returning a back pocket at score 0.906 as the garment mask — so a per-pocket reference frame is what lets a person adjudicate a suspect mask later instead of guessing.
- [ ] `INTAKE.FEATURE.BACK_POCKET.POCKET_BACK_RIGHT.I01` (1/1, conditional, has_back_pockets and has_right_back_pocket)
      Garment-RIGHT back pocket (image RIGHT in the back-up lay), framed identically to
      the left pocket shot so the two can be compared directly: same standoff, same rule
      position relative to the pocket, same orientation.
      *why:* Deliberately paired with the left pocket. Left/right asymmetry in stitch position and fade is common on used garments and is the cheapest available check on whether a post-wash difference is a real effect: an effect that appears on one pocket and not its mirror is either a genuine asymmetry recorded here at intake, or an artefact.

### Garment intake — BACK up, lay 1, mount_overhead_locked, main lens

- [ ] `INTAKE.WHOLE.BACK_OVERHEAD_ASIS` (1/1, required)
      As INTAKE.WHOLE.FRONT_OVERHEAD_ASIS but back up. Flip the garment about its LONG
      axis so the waistband stays at the top of frame; this puts the garment's left leg on
      the image LEFT (it was on the image RIGHT in the front-up lay). Do not flip about
      the horizontal axis.
      *why:* The enumeration reference for every back-panel feature instance, and the arrival-condition record for the side that carries the back pockets, yoke and — on this project's own pilot candidate — the painted print. It exists separately from the front frame because an instance ordinal must be assigned in the frame where the instance is actually visible.

- [ ] `BEFORE.HEM.LEFT.SELVEDGE_AT_HEM.MACRO` (1/1, conditional, has_selvedge)
      PARAMETERISED OVER LEG: the generator expands LEFT to LEFT and RIGHT (and left in
      region_id to left/right). Fill the frame with about 100 mm centred on the point
      where the selvedge outseam runs into the hem, so that the selvedge's woven edge, its
      coloured line if present, and the hem fold are all visible. Loop tape flat 10 mm
      outboard, graduations legible.
      *why:* A selvedge outseam terminates the hem loop in a self-finished woven edge that does not fray, so at that junction the post-wash raw cut edge meets a non-fraying boundary.       centred on loop position Pc, optical axis perpendicular to the fabric plane,

      back to P01 are shot with the leg turned back-up, the tape coordinate continuing

      back to P01 are shot with the leg turned back-up, the tape coordinate continuing

- [ ] `BEFORE.HEM.LEFT.INSEAM_JUNCTION.MACRO` (1/2, required)
      Fill the frame with about 100 mm of hem edge CENTRED on the point where the inseam

      unrolled cuff depth in mm from the tape.

- [ ] `BEFORE.HEM.LEFT.WEAR.INN.MACRO.I01` (1/1, conditional, n_distressing > 0)
      PARAMETERISED OVER LEG AND INSTANCE. The generator emits one instance per counted
      feature occurrence located within 120 mm of the hem, with Inn replaced by the zero-
      padded instance index. Instance indices are assigned from the record's
      existing_damage_annotations array order where the occurrence is already annotated
      there, and otherwise from an instance table the pilot ledger maintains keyed by
      (leg, feature_key, index), each row carrying a written 'saw' sentence. Frame about
      100 mm centred on the occurrence with the loop tape in frame so its loop coordinate
      is readable, and the hem edge visible along one side of the frame.
      *why:* Pre-existing damage, repairs, stains, paint or printed fade near the hem sit inside the region the post-wash loop map will measure, and hem_roughness cannot tell a pre-existing hole or a paint edge from a wash-produced fringe. Every such occurrence must have a dated before-image at measurement resolution with its loop coordinate recorded, or the corresponding post-wash positions are confounded and must be refused rather than reported.
